Zuhayr is praising a brave man, and he borrowed for him the name of the lion by way of metaphor (tasrihiyyah), and "hunting" is a complement (tarshih). "Athar" is the name of a place. That is: a brave man in 'Athar kills men when he "lies," i.e., when the strong horseman becomes cowardly and weak before his rivals in war; he is "truthful," his resolve is executed, and he kills his opponent. In the verse there is the antithesis (tibaq) between "truthful" and "lied," and it is among the elegant features of speech.

That is: when it occurs there will be no return or reversal for it. "Lowering, raising" (khafidah rafi'ah): i.e., "it is lowering and raising," lifting some peoples and abasing others. This is either a description of its severity, since great occurrences are like that, in which some people rise to high ranks and others are brought low; or because the wretched are brought down to the depths and the blessed raised to the degrees; or because it shakes things and removes them from their places, lowering some and raising others. [This is] when the sky splits asunder [Qur'an 55:37], the stars scatter and fall, and the mountains are set in motion so that they pass through the air like clouds. It is recited "khafidatan rafi'atan" in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

"Ruijjat" — it was shaken with a violent shaking until everything upon it, mountain and building, is demolished. "Bussat al-jibal" — the mountains are crumbled and pulverized until they become like flour (al-sawiq), or it is from "bass al-'anam" when he drove them; like His saying: "and the mountains are set in motion" [78:20]. "Munbathth" — scattered. It is recited with the feminine ta' ("tabaththu"), i.e., cut off. It is also recited "rujjat" and "bussat," meaning: they were agitated and went away.

In the speech of the daughter of al-Khass: "her eye is hajah, her flanks are raj, and she walks and fajj." If you ask: With what is "idha rujjat" in the accusative? I say: It is a substitute (badal) for "idha waqa'at." It may also be governed by "khafidah rafi'ah": i.e., it lowers and raises at the time the earth is shaken and the mountains are crumbled, because at that time what is high is lowered and what is low is raised. "Azwajan" — kinds, categories. Groups that are together with one another, or that are mentioned together, are called "azwaj" (pairs).

Meccan [except verses 81 and 82, which are Medinan]; its verses are 96, and it is said 97 verses. [It was revealed after Ta-Ha.] In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

"When the Event occurs" (al-waqi'ah). Like your saying: "The occurrence occurred" (kanat al-ka'inah) and "the happening happened" (huddithat al-hadithah). What is meant is the Resurrection. It is described as "occurring" because it will occur without doubt, as if it were said: "When that which must occur occurs." The occurrence of a matter is its descent.

It is said: "What I was awaiting has occurred," meaning: what I was waiting for to descend has descended.

If you ask: With what is "when" (idha) in the accusative?

I say: It is governed by "laysa" (there is not), as in your saying: "On Friday I have no business." Or it is governed by something omitted, meaning: "When it occurs, such-and-such will be the case." Or by the implied "remember" (udhkur). "No soul will then deny its occurrence" (kadhibah): i.e., at the time it occurs there will be no soul that lies about God and denies the unseen, for every soul at that time will be believing, truthful and affirming. Most souls today are liars and deniers, as in His saying: "Then when they saw Our might they said: 'We believe in God alone, and we reject what we used to associate with Him.' But their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might" [40:84–85], and His saying: "Those who disbelieve will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes upon them suddenly" [22:55]. The lam [in "laysa lil-waqi'atihā kadhibah"] is like it in His saying: "O, would that I had sent forth [good deeds] for my life" [89:24]. Or: there will be no soul that will deny it and say to it: "You will not be," as many souls today deny it, saying to it: "You will not be." Or it is from the saying: "His soul lied to him about the great matter," when it encouraged him to undertake it and told him: "You can bear it and what is beyond it," so he confronted it without heed; the meaning being that it is an occurrence that cannot be borne in its severity and dreadfulness. And there will be no soul then that will speak to its owner as it speaks to him at the time of great affairs and makes their endurance and bearing seem fair to him, because on that Day they will be weaker and more humiliated than that. Do you not see His saying: "like scattered moths" [101:4]? The moth is a figure for weakness.

It is also said: "kadhibah" is a verbal noun like "al-'aqibah," in the sense of "denial," from your saying: "He charged at his opponent, but did not lie" (fa-ma kadhaba), i.e., he did not become cowardly or falter. Its real sense is: he did not lie to himself regarding what it told him of his ability to bear it and his advancing upon it. Zuhayr said:

Then the companions of the right hand: how fortunate are the companions of the right hand! And the companions of the left hand: how wretched are the companions of the left hand! (Wait—this is the translation of the verse's meaning; the passage itself follows.)

Correction, translating the passage as given:

Then the companions of the right (al-maymana), those who are given their records in their right hands; and the companions of the left (al-mash'ama), those who are given them in their left hands. Or: the companions of the lofty station and the companions of the lowly station, from your saying, "So-and-so is on my right (bi-l-yamin), so-and-so is on my left (bi-l-shimal)," when you describe them as high or low in your estimation. This is because of their taking omens from the right (tayammun bi-l-mayamin) and their taking bad omens from the left (tashå'um bi-l-shamā'il), and because of their optimism with the sāniḥ (the gazelle or bird that passes from your left to your right, a good omen) and their pessimism at the bārih (its opposite). Thus al-Jawharī, in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. For this reason they derived the name for the right (al-yamīn) from prosperity (al-yumn), and called the left the ominous (al-shu'mā).

It has also been said: the companions of the right and the companions of the left are the companions of blessing and of misfortune, because the fortunate are "blessed" (ḥayāmīn) through their obedience, and the wretched are "ominous" for themselves through their disobedience.

It has also been said: the people of the Garden are taken to the right (dhāt al-yamīn), and the people of the Fire are taken to the left (dhāt al-shimāl).

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "Mā" is for wonder at the state of the two groups..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: He chose what is the preferred reading, because it is more firmly grounded in eloquence. But there remains a point to note about the difference between what is mentioned about the foremost (al-sabiqun) and about the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), even though each of them is intended to magnify and awe the state of those mentioned. So we say: the magnification conveyed by ﴿al-sabiqun﴾ is more eloquent than its counterpart, because what this conveys is that the matter of the foremost and the greatness of their station is hardly hidden, and that the listener's bewilderment about it is well known. As for what is mentioned in ﴿fa-ashab al-maymanah ma ashab al-maymanah﴾, it is a magnification that overwhelms the listener with something he has no prior knowledge of. Do you not see how the description of the foremost was preceded by ﴿ulaika al-muqarrabun﴾, combining the demonstrative pointing to a known thing with a predicate about it, ﴿al-muqarrabun﴾, defined with the definite article of prior reference? Nothing like this is mentioned in the description of the companions of the right, which begins with ﴿fi sidrin makhdud﴾.]].

﴿Wa-l-sabiqun al-sabiqun﴾: the meaning is, "What are they?" And "the foremost, the foremost" means: the foremost are those whose state you have come to know and whose description has reached you, like the saying "Abdullah, Abdullah" [in the sense of "the true servant of Allah"]. And like the verse of Abu al-Najm: "I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is (my) poetry" [...] [[Abu al-Najm's verses: "I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is poetry; by God, how wondrous is what my breast conceals. My eye sleeps while my heart travels by night among the goblins in a barren land." These verses are by Abu al-Najm al-Ijli. He means: I am the one known for eloquence among people, like a well-known flag. "My poetry" means: the eloquent one known as the poetry of Abu al-Najm. When the subject and predicate, or the condition and consequence, are identical, the sentence implies hyperbole in magnification or in belittlement. What is here is of the first kind, as the context shows. It also claims that the peak of greatness lies in the man named Abu al-Najm, and the peak of eloquence in the poetry attributed to him. "Al-durr" means milk, but what is meant here is work and craft: that is, "by God, my product," meaning that it is great. "Jan al-layl" means the night became dark. "Al-nabt" means the plant grew long and dense. "Al-dhubab" means its sounds multiplied. "Janna-hu al-layl" means it covered him, and "ajanna-hu al-sadr" means he concealed it. "Ma" here is for expressing wonder. "Ajann" is a verb of wonder, meaning: how great is the thing that made my breast embrace strange meanings. It is possible that "ma" is in apposition to "durri." "Ajann" is a past verb serving as a relative clause or attribute of it. "Mu'adi" means my heart or my mind. "Yasra" means he travels by night, meaning my thought spends the night as if it went with goblins in an open land without plants, due to its remoteness in meanings. The second verse is an explanation of the first.]]. It is as if he said: "And my poetry, which has reached you, and whose eloquence and skill you have heard of." The foremost have been made an emphasis. ﴿Ulaika al-muqarrabun﴾ [is] the predicate, though that is not the right reading. Some stopped at ﴿wa-l-sabiqun﴾ and began a new sentence with ﴿al-sabiqun ulaika al-muqarrabun﴾, but the correct reading is to stop at the second, because it completes the sentence and corresponds to ﴿ma ashab al-maymanah﴾ and ﴿ma ashab al-mash'amah﴾.

﴿Al-muqarrabun fi jannat al-na'im﴾: those whose ranks in Paradise are brought near to the Throne and whose stations are elevated.

It is read ﴿fi jannat al-na'im﴾ [in the singular]. ﴿Al-thullah﴾ is a large multitude of people. [A poet] said:

"And there came to them a multitude of the Khindif clan, with an army like a flood current, foaming."

[[The verse: "And there came to them a multitude of the Khindif clan, with an army like a flood current, foaming." He says: there came to them a group of people belonging to Khindif, the woman of Ilyas ibn Mudar. His saying "bi-jaysh" is by way of abstraction (tajrid), as if he extracted from the multitude an army other than it, as exaggeration in number. It is possible that the "ba'" means "with" or "in," because the army is broader than the multitude. "Jaysh" comes from "jasha," meaning it moved and churned, as if it were boiling. "Tayyar" is strongly flowing water. "Min" is explanatory or partitive. "Mazid" means that its foam rose high on its surface due to its abundance and overflowing.]]

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿wa-qalilun min al-akhirin﴾: it suffices as proof of the multitude [of the foremost]. ﴿Thullah﴾ comes from ﴿thalm﴾, meaning breaking, just as ﴿ummah﴾ comes from ﴿umm﴾, meaning a wound in the skull; it is as if it is a group broken off and cut away from people. The meaning is that the foremost among the earlier ones are many: they are the nations from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Wa-qalilun min al-akhirin﴾ are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that ﴿min al-awwalin﴾ refers to the forerunners of this community and ﴿min al-akhirin﴾ to its later members. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Both groups are from my community." [[Narrated by al-Tabari and Ibn 'Adi from the transmission of Aban from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, who said regarding this verse, "A multitude of the earlier ones and a multitude of the later ones," that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Both of them are from my community." Aban is Ibn Abi 'Ayyash, who is abandoned (matruk). It was also transmitted by Ishaq, with a chain to al-Tayalisi, Ibrahim al-Harbi and al-Tabarani, from the transmission of Zayd ibn Sahban from Abu Bakrah, as a marfu' and mawquf report. The mawquf is more correct. And it is weak.]] If you say: how can He say "wa-qalilun min al-akhirin" and then say "wa-thullatun min al-akhirin"? I say: the first refers to the foremost, and the second to the companions of the right, who will be numerous from both the earlier and the later ones together.

If you say: it is reported that when this was revealed it grieved the Muslims, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept returning to his Lord until ﴿thullatun min al-awwalin wa-thullatun min al-akhirin﴾ was revealed. I say: this is not sound, for two reasons. First, this verse clearly refers to the foremost, and likewise the second refers clearly to the companions of [[his saying "likewise the second refers to the companions of the right," meaning its reference is apparent. (ع)]] the right. Do you not see how the companions of the right were joined to the foremost in both their description and their promise? Second, abrogation (naskh) is not permissible in reports (akhbar). It is reported from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: the foremost of earlier nations are more numerous than the foremost of our nation, and the followers of earlier nations are like the followers of this nation.

﴿Thullah﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are a multitude ﴿mawdunah﴾, woven with gold, interlaced with pearls and rubies, their parts sunk into one another as the rings of a coat of mail are interlocked.

[[His saying "mawdunah" is in some dictionaries "ramalat al-hasir," meaning I wove it. And also "saffaftu al-khus," meaning I wove the palm fibers. (ع)]]

Al-A'sha said:

"And from the weaving of David, interlaced ones, drawn along with the tribe, caravan after caravan."

[[This is al-A'sha, describing coats of mail, and making them the weaving of our master David is hyperbole for the excellence of their craftsmanship, because he wove them by the command of God and His teaching to him. "Mawdunah" means their parts are inserted into one another, so they are tightly woven. "Tusa" means their wearers are drawn along with the tribe. "Ir" with a fatha means a lord, meaning lord after lord, arrayed, and "ir" is also applied to a bird that flies above the moving caravan, but that meaning is far-fetched here.]]

It is said: "mutawasilah," meaning close to one another.

﴿Muttaki'in﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿'ala﴾, and it is the operating element of it. That is: they settle upon them reclining, ﴿mutaqabilin﴾, not looking at the napes of one another. They are described with good companionship, refinement of character and good manners.

﴿Mukhalladun﴾: remaining forever, always, in the form of youths and the limit of adolescence, not changing from it. It was said: "wearing earrings," since "khaldah" means an earring. It was said: they are the children of the people of this world, who had no good deeds for which they would be rewarded, nor evil deeds for which they would be punished. This is reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and from al-Hasan.

In a hadith: "The children of the unbelievers are servants of the people of Paradise." [[Narrated by al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat from the transmission of 'Abbad ibn Mansur from Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi from Samurah ibn Jundub, who said: "We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the children of the polytheists, and he said: They are servants of the people of Paradise." Al-Bazzar also transmitted it from 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, and al-Tayalisi, al-Tabarani and Abu Ya'la from the transmission of Yazid al-Raqqashi, both from Anas with this wording and more complete. I say: it may be contradicted by the hadith of Samurah in Sahih al-Bukhari, where he saw people's children under a tree, cared for by Ibrahim (peace be upon him). He said: we said, "And the children of the polytheists?" He said: "And the children of the polytheists," narrated with this wording. It can be reconciled between them, since there is no contradiction, because it is possible that they are in this state in the barzakh, and then after settling they will settle in Paradise as servants of its people.]]

﴿Al-akwab﴾: vessels without handles and spouts. ﴿Al-abariq﴾: those with spouts. ﴿La yusda'una 'anha﴾: they will not be afflicted with headache because of them; the literal sense is that their headache does not arise from it. Or: they will not be separated from it. Mujahid read ﴿la yusdda'un﴾, meaning they will not split apart or disperse, like His saying ﴿yawma'idhin yassaddaʿun﴾, which is read "yassadda'un": that is, they will not cause one another to split apart, or separate one another.

﴿Yatakhayyarun﴾: they take its choicest and best. ﴿Yashtahun﴾: they desire. It is read: "wa-luhumi tayrin" [with a different reading]. It is read ﴿wa-hurun 'in﴾, in the nominative, as "wa-fiha hurun 'in," like the verse in the Book (Sibawayh):

"Except for the stationary hearth-stones whose embers are ashes."

[[The verse: "Badat wa-ghayyara ayatuhunna ma'a al-bali, illa rawakida jamrihinna haba'." And "Mushajjaj" is either equal in its temple, so it appeared, and "ghayyara sarrahu al-maghra'": the desert after its inhabitants... This is attributed to al-Shammakh, though it is also attributed to Dhu al-Rummah, and it is among the verses of the Kitab. "Badda, yabidd" means perished, died. "Al-ayy" is the plural of "ayah," a sign. "Al-rawakid" are the three stones on which the cooking pot is placed. "Al-haba'" is dust mixed with earth. "Al-mushajjaj" is an attribute used as a noun for the tent peg whose head is cracked from pounding. So what protrudes around its head resembles the temple, which is the hair at the sides of the head. "Sawa' al-shay'" is its middle. It is also narrated as "ghayyab" instead of "ghayyara." "Al-sar" with or without hamza means what remains. "Al-maghra'" is land whose soil is mixed with stones and pebbles. He says: the dwellings have perished for you and their traces are effaced, and nothing remains except the place of fire and the remnant of the tent peg. It is also narrated "rawakida" in the accusative, coordinating the nominative with the accusative based on the meaning.]]

Or it is in coordination with ﴿wildan﴾, and in the genitive it is coordinated with ﴿jannat al-na'im﴾, as if he said: they are in gardens of delight, and fruit, and meat, and ﴿hur﴾. Or it is coordinated with ﴿akwab﴾, because the meaning of ﴿yatufu 'alayhim wildanun mukhalladun bi-akwab﴾ is that they enjoy themselves with cups. In the accusative, it means: and they are given ﴿hurun﴾ as a reward; it is an object of purpose: that is, all of this is done to them as a recompense for their deeds.

﴿Salaman salaman﴾: either it is a substitute for ﴿qilan﴾, by the evidence of His saying ﴿la yasma'una fiha laghwan illa salaman﴾, or it is a direct object of ﴿qilan﴾, meaning: they will not hear in it vain talk, except that they say "Peace, peace." The meaning is that they spread the greeting among themselves, so they greet one another with peace after peace. It is also read "salamun salamun," as a reported speech.

In a hadith: "The children of the unbelievers are servants of the people of Paradise." [[Narrated by al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat from the transmission of 'Abbad ibn Mansur from Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi from Samurah ibn Jundub, who said: "We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the children of the polytheists, and he said: They are servants of the people of Paradise." "Except for the stationary hearth-stones whose embers are ashes."

[[The verse: "Badat wa-ghayyara ayatuhunna ma'a al-bali, illa rawakida jamrihinna haba'." Or it is in coordination with ﴿wildan﴾, and in the genitive it is coordinated with ﴿jannat al-na'im﴾, as if he said: they are in gardens of delight, and fruit, and meat, and ﴿hur﴾. The meaning is that they spread the greeting among themselves, so they greet one another with peace after peace. It is also read "salamun salamun," as a reported speech.

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words: "Mā" is for wonder at the state of the two groups..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: He chose what is the preferred reading, because it is more firmly grounded in eloquence. But there remains a point to note about the difference between what is mentioned about the foremost (al-sabiqun) and about the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), even though each of them is intended to magnify and awe the state of those mentioned. So we say: the magnification conveyed by ﴿al-sabiqun﴾ is more eloquent than its counterpart, because what this conveys is that the matter of the foremost and the greatness of their station is hardly hidden, and that the listener's bewilderment about it is well known. As for what is mentioned in ﴿fa-ashab al-maymanah ma ashab al-maymanah﴾, it is a magnification that overwhelms the listener with something he has no prior knowledge of. Do you not see how the description of the foremost was preceded by ﴿ulaika al-muqarrabun﴾, combining the demonstrative pointing to a known thing with a predicate about it, ﴿al-muqarrabun﴾, defined with the definite article of prior reference? ﴿Wa-l-sabiqun al-sabiqun﴾: the meaning is, "What are they?" And "the foremost, the foremost" means: the foremost are those whose state you have come to know and whose description has reached you, like the saying "Abdullah, Abdullah" [in the sense of "the true servant of Allah"]. And like the verse of Abu al-Najm: "I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is (my) poetry" [...] [[Abu al-Najm's verses: "I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is poetry; by God, how wondrous is what my breast conceals. My eye sleeps while my heart travels by night among the goblins in a barren land." These verses are by Abu al-Najm al-Ijli. He means: I am the one known for eloquence among people, like a well-known flag. "My poetry" means: the eloquent one known as the poetry of Abu al-Najm. When the subject and predicate, or the condition and consequence, are identical, the sentence implies hyperbole in magnification or in belittlement. What is here is of the first kind, as the context shows. It also claims that the peak of greatness lies in the man named Abu al-Najm, and the peak of eloquence in the poetry attributed to him. "Al-durr" means milk, but what is meant here is work and craft: that is, "by God, my product," meaning that it is great. "Jan al-layl" means the night became dark. "Al-nabt" means the plant grew long and dense. "Al-dhubab" means its sounds multiplied. "Janna-hu al-layl" means it covered him, and "ajanna-hu al-sadr" means he concealed it. "Ma" here is for expressing wonder. "Ajann" is a verb of wonder, meaning: how great is the thing that made my breast embrace strange meanings. It is possible that "ma" is in apposition to "durri." "Ajann" is a past verb serving as a relative clause or attribute of it. "Mu'adi" means my heart or my mind. "Yasra" means he travels by night, meaning my thought spends the night as if it went with goblins in an open land without plants, due to its remoteness in meanings. The second verse is an explanation of the first.]]. It is as if he said: "And my poetry, which has reached you, and whose eloquence and skill you have heard of." The foremost have been made an emphasis. ﴿Ulaika al-muqarrabun﴾ [is] the predicate, though that is not the right reading. Some stopped at ﴿wa-l-sabiqun﴾ and began a new sentence with ﴿al-sabiqun ulaika al-muqarrabun﴾, but the correct reading is to stop at the second, because it completes the sentence and corresponds to ﴿ma ashab al-maymanah﴾ and ﴿ma ashab al-mash'amah﴾.

﴿Al-muqarrabun fi jannat al-na'im﴾: those whose ranks in Paradise are brought near to the Throne and whose stations are elevated.

It is read ﴿fi jannat al-na'im﴾ [in the singular]. ﴿Al-thullah﴾ is a large multitude of people. [A poet] said:

"And there came to them a multitude of the Khindif clan, with an army like a flood current, foaming."

[[The verse: "And there came to them a multitude of the Khindif clan, with an army like a flood current, foaming." He says: there came to them a group of people belonging to Khindif, the woman of Ilyas ibn Mudar. His saying "bi-jaysh" is by way of abstraction (tajrid), as if he extracted from the multitude an army other than it, as exaggeration in number. It is possible that the "ba'" means "with" or "in," because the army is broader than the multitude. "Jaysh" comes from "jasha," meaning it moved and churned, as if it were boiling. I say: the first refers to the foremost, and the second to the companions of the right, who will be numerous from both the earlier and the later ones together.

If you say: it is reported that when this was revealed it grieved the Muslims, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept returning to his Lord until ﴿thullatun min al-awwalin wa-thullatun min al-akhirin﴾ was revealed. Al-A'sha said:

It is laden with fruit, its branches bent by the abundance of its load, from *khadd al-ghusn*, when it is bent while still green.

**Al-Talh** is the banana tree. It was also said that it is the *shajar Umm Ghaylan*, which has abundant, fragrant blossoms. Al-Suddi said: it is a tree resembling the *talh* of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. It is reported from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he recited *wa-talʿin* (and clustered fruit) and said *wa-ma sha'n al-talh* (what is the matter with the talh). Ibn ʿAbbas said something similar.

**Al-Mandud** is that which is stacked (*nuḍida*) with fruit from its base to its top, so it has no visible trunk. [In al-Sihah, it is what is piled one upon another. (ʿ)]

﴿And shade extended﴾ [Q. 56:30]: extended, spread out, not contracting, like the shade between the break of dawn and sunrise.

﴿And water poured out﴾ [Q. 56:31]: flowing for them wherever they wish and however they wish, without any toil. It was said: it constantly flows, never ceasing. It was also said: it is poured out and runs upon the ground without a channel.

﴿Neither cut off﴾ [Q. 56:33]: they are constant and never cease at any time, unlike the fruits of this world.

﴿Nor forbidden﴾ [Q. 56:33]: they are not withheld from anyone who wishes to take them in any way, nor are they prohibited, as the gardens of this world are prohibited.

It was recited: *wa-fākihatun kathīratun* (and abundant fruit) in the nominative, meaning "and there is abundant fruit." Similarly, *ḥūrun ʿīn* (and wide-eyed maidens) [Q. 56:22].

**Furush** is the plural of *firāsh*. It was also recited as *wa-farsh* with the lighter pronunciation.

﴿Raised up﴾ [Q. 56:34]: arranged in layers until they are elevated. Or it means raised upon couches. It was also said that it refers to women, because a woman is referred to by the word *firāsh* (bedding). [It is] raised upon couches. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They and their spouses, in shade, reclining upon couches﴾ [Q. 36:56]. This is supported by His words: ﴿Indeed, We have created them with a special creation﴾ [Q. 56:35]. According to the first interpretation, the pronoun for them is implied, because mention of the *furush*, which are the beds, indicates them. ﴿We created them with a special creation﴾ means We began their creation anew, without birth. So it may mean "those whose creation was initiated," or "those whose creation was renewed."

It is reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [the Tha'labi reported it in full through al-Hasan ibn ʿAlawiyya al-Qattan, from Isma'il ibn ʿIsa, from al-Musayyib ibn Sharik, but he raised only the story of ʿAʾisha to the Prophet. Through Ghunjar, Isma'il ibn Abi al-Ba'd narrated to us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, from Umm Salama, traced back to the Prophet, without the story of ʿAʾisha. al-Tabari, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, through ʿUmar ibn Hashim al-Bayruti, from Sulayman ibn Abi Karima, from Hisham, from al-Hasan, from his mother, from Umm Salama, who said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah, tell me about the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿ʿuruban atrabā﴾ [Q. 56:37]," and he mentioned it. In it: "He made them virgins, loving and devoted to their husbands, of the same age, born at one time." al-Tirmidhi narrated part of it through Musa ibn ʿUbayda, from Yazid al-Raqqashi, and declared him weak.] that Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, asked him about the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿We created them with a special creation﴾. He said: "O Umm Salama, they are those who passed away in this worldly abode as old women, white-haired and with discharge in their eyes. Allah made them, after old age, [of the same age] (*atrāban*) at one birth, in equal youth. Whenever their husbands came to them, they found them virgins." When ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, heard this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), she said: "Alas, my pain!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no pain there." An old woman said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Ask Allah to admit me into Paradise," and he said: "Indeed, old women will not enter Paradise." She turned away weeping, so he, peace be upon him, said: "Inform her that she will not be an old woman on that day." [al-Tirmidhi reported it in al-Shama'il through the narration of Mubarak ibn Fudala, from al-Hasan, as a mursal report, and its context is more complete. It has other chains. Among them, in al-Ba'th, al-Bayhaqi narrated through Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Mujahid, from ʿAʾisha. Among them, in al-Awsat, through Mas'ada ibn al-Yasa', from Sa'id, from Qatada, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from ʿAʾisha. Khaija ibn Mus'ab narrated it from Sa'id, from Qatada, from Anas. All of them are weak.] He recited the verse: ﴿ʿUruban﴾ [Q. 56:37]. It was recited as *ʿarab* with the lighter pronunciation. It is the plural of *ʿarūb*, the woman who is affectionate to her husband and good in her marital conduct. ﴿Atrāban﴾ [Q. 56:37]: equal in age, daughters of thirty-three, and their husbands likewise.

It is reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The people of Paradise will enter Paradise beardless, smooth-bodied, with white skin, curly hair, and kohl-lined eyes, aged thirty-three." [Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated it through Hammad ibn Salama, from ʿAli ibn Zayd, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from Abu Hurayra, in this form. Al-Suddi said: it is a tree resembling the *talh* of this world, but it has fruit sweeter than honey. **Al-Mandud** is that which is stacked (*nuḍida*) with fruit from its base to its top, so it has no visible trunk. [In al-Sihah, it is what is piled one upon another. (ʿ)]

Fī samūmin (in the scorching heat of fire that penetrates the pores pores) wa-ḥamīmin (and boiling water, extremely hot) wa-ẓillin min yaḥmūmin (and a shade of black smoke, pitch-black), lā bāridin wa-lā karīmin (neither cool nor generous). He negated the two attributes of shade from it, meaning: it is a shade, but not like other shades. He named it a shade, then negated from it the coolness, the refreshment and the benefit of a shade for one who takes refuge in it from the harm of heat; and that is its "generosity" (karam), so as to annihilate what the connotation of "shade" carries of finding rest in it. The meaning is that it is a shade that is hot and harmful. However, negation in such cases has a force that affirmation does not have. There is also in this a mockery of the people of the left (aṣḥāb al-shu'ma), and that they do not deserve the cool, generous shade which is for their opposites in Paradise. It has been read lā bāridun wa-lā karīmun with the nominative, meaning: it is not so.

Al-ḥinth (ḥinth) is the great sin, and from it comes their saying: "The boy has reached al-ḥinth," i.e., puberty and the time of being held accountable for sins. And from it: "He broke (ḥanitha) his oath," in contrast to "he fulfilled (barra) it." It is said: "taḥannatha" when one commits sin and becomes scrupulous. A'a-ābā'unā: the interrogative hamza has entered upon the conjunction particle. If you ask: how is coordination with the pronoun in lamab'ūthūna good without emphasis by "naḥnu"? I say: it is good because of the intervening element, which is the hamza, just as it is good in His saying, "neither we nor our fathers had associated [anything]" (ﷻ), because of the emphatic negating particle lā. It has been read: aw ābā'unā. It has also been read: la-majmū'ūna (and the gathered ones) ilā mīqāti yawmin ma'lūmin (to the appointed time of a known day): to the time that the world was fixed for, a known day, and the idafa (construct) is in the sense of "min," like "a ring of silver." Al-mīqāt is that by which a thing is timed, i.e., its limit. From it come the mawāqīt al-iḥrām (the stations of ihram), which are the limits that one who wishes to enter Mecca may not pass except in the state of ihram.

Ayyuhā al-ḍāllūna (O you who went astray from guidance), al-mukadhdhibūna bil-ba'th (who deny the resurrection), and they are the people of Mecca and those in a similar condition. Min shajarin min zaqqūmin: the first min is for the beginning of the extent, and the second is to explain and specify the tree. He made the pronoun referring to the tree feminine according to the meaning, and masculine according to the wording, in His saying minhā and 'alayhi. Whoever reads min shajarin min zaqqūmin has made both pronouns refer to the tree, and the second was mentioned by way of interpreting zaqqūm, since it explains it and is of its meaning.

Shurba al-hīm (drinking as the thirsty camels drink). It has been read with the three vowel forms; the fatḥa and ḍamma are both verbal nouns (maṣdars). It is reported from Ja'far al-Ṣādiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he read it with fatḥa on the shīn, meaning "the act of drinking." As for the kasra, it means "that which is drunk," i.e., what the hīm drink. Al-hīm are camels afflicted with al-hiyām, a disease from which they drink and are never quenched. It is the plural of ahyam and hayma'. Dhu al-Rumma said:

"So she became like the hayma' (thirst-stricken camel), for neither cool water satisfies its thirst, nor is its longing ended."

[Dhu al-Rumma's verses, with commentary: "And Mayy provided us at the parting with a kiss, a long-lasting bond of needs, whose sickness is prolonged... So she became like the hayma', to which neither cool water brings relief... nor is its longing ended." He says: she provided us, i.e., made our provision Mayy's kiss at departure, and that kiss was the bond of needs and causes of longing for union. "'Alā'iqu" is a raised predicate or a accusative apposition. "Al-saqām" (sickness) is like kalām, and "suqm" like ta'ab, and "suqm" like bukhl, a verbal noun of saqima; i.e., its toil is long-lasting and does not heal. The camel is called ahyam and the she-camel hayma', when the hiyām afflicts them; it is a disease, caused by which the hearts of camels boil like extreme thirst. His saying "lā al-mā'u mubrad" is a resumptive clause explaining the point of similarity, or a circumstantial clause: water does not cool their thirst, nor is it ended for them, i.e., their longing does not stop, so I am likewise: no union that would heal me, nor does despair kill me. It is also narrated: "wa-lā yuqḍā 'alā hiyāmihā," and perhaps its meaning: neither water cools the burning that I have received from it, nor does the longing that I received from it kill me; but the first is more firmly established and better in meaning.]

It was also said: al-hīm are sands. Its basis is that it is the plural of al-hiyām with a fatḥa on the hā', which is sand that does not hold together, pluralized on the pattern fa'l like saḥāb and suḥb; then it was lightened and treated as the plural abyaḍ. The meaning: there is imposed upon them from hunger what compels them to eat the zaqqūm, which is like molten dregs. When they have filled their bellies from it, there is imposed upon them from thirst what compels them to drink the ḥamīm that cuts their intestines, so they drink it as the hīm drink water.

If you ask: how is the coordination of "drinkers" upon "drinkers" correct, when they are of the same subject and the same two attributes are identical, so that it would be coordinating a thing upon itself? I say: they are not identical, in that their being drinkers of the ḥamīm in the state it is in—extreme heat and cutting the intestines—is a strange matter, and their drinking it as the hīm drink water is also a strange matter; so they are two different attributes.

Nuzl: the provision prepared for a guest out of honor. There is mockery in it, as in His saying, "so give them the good news of a painful punishment" (ﷻ), and like the saying of Abū al-Shi'r al-Ḍabbī:

"And when the tyrant came upon us with his army, we made the spears and the sharp swords his nuzl (welcome)."

[The explanation of this witness has been given in the first part, p. 458; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]

It has been read: nuzluhum with light pronunciation.

It is the plural of ahyam and hayma'. Dhu al-Rumma said:

[Dhu al-Rumma's verses, with commentary: "And Mayy provided us at the parting with a kiss, a long-lasting bond of needs, whose sickness is prolonged... So she became like the hayma', to which neither cool water brings relief... nor is its longing ended." "'Alā'iqu" is a raised predicate or a accusative apposition. "Al-saqām" (sickness) is like kalām, and "suqm" like ta'ab, and "suqm" like bukhl, a verbal noun of saqima; i.e., its toil is long-lasting and does not heal. The camel is called ahyam and the she-camel hayma', when the hiyām afflicts them; it is a disease, caused by which the hearts of camels boil like extreme thirst. His saying "lā al-mā'u mubrad" is a resumptive clause explaining the point of similarity, or a circumstantial clause: water does not cool their thirst, nor is it ended for them, i.e., their longing does not stop, so I am likewise: no union that would heal me, nor does despair kill me. It is also narrated: "wa-lā yuqḍā 'alā hiyāmihā," and perhaps its meaning: neither water cools the burning that I have received from it, nor does the longing that I received from it kill me; but the first is more firmly established and better in meaning.]

It was also said: al-hīm are sands. Its basis is that it is the plural of al-hiyām with a fatḥa on the hā', which is sand that does not hold together, pluralized on the pattern fa'l like saḥāb and suḥb; then it was lightened and treated as the plural abyaḍ. The meaning: there is imposed upon them from hunger what compels them to eat the zaqqūm, which is like molten dregs. When they have filled their bellies from it, there is imposed upon them from thirst what compels them to drink the ḥamīm that cuts their intestines, so they drink it as the hīm drink water.

If you ask: how is the coordination of "drinkers" upon "drinkers" correct, when they are of the same subject and the same two attributes are identical, so that it would be coordinating a thing upon itself? I say: they are not identical, in that their being drinkers of the ḥamīm in the state it is in—extreme heat and cutting the intestines—is a strange matter, and their drinking it as the hīm drink water is also a strange matter; so they are two different attributes.

Nuzl: the provision prepared for a guest out of honor. There is mockery in it, as in His saying, "so give them the good news of a painful punishment" (ﷻ), and like the saying of Abū al-Shi'r al-Ḍabbī:

"And when the tyrant came upon us with his army, we made the spears and the sharp swords his nuzl (welcome)."

[The explanation of this witness has been given in the first part, p. 458; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]

It has been read: nuzluhum with light pronunciation.

Fī samūmin (in the scorching heat of fire that penetrates the pores pores) wa-ḥamīmin (and boiling water, extremely hot) wa-ẓillin min yaḥmūmin (and a shade of black smoke, pitch-black), lā bāridin wa-lā karīmin (neither cool nor generous). He negated the two attributes of shade from it, meaning: it is a shade, but not like other shades. He named it a shade, then negated from it the coolness, the refreshment and the benefit of a shade for one who takes refuge in it from the harm of heat; and that is its "generosity" (karam), so as to annihilate what the connotation of "shade" carries of finding rest in it. The meaning is that it is a shade that is hot and harmful. However, negation in such cases has a force that affirmation does not have. There is also in this a mockery of the people of the left (aṣḥāb al-shu'ma), and that they do not deserve the cool, generous shade which is for their opposites in Paradise. It has been read lā bāridun wa-lā karīmun with the nominative, meaning: it is not so.

Al-ḥinth (ḥinth) is the great sin, and from it comes their saying: "The boy has reached al-ḥinth," i.e., puberty and the time of being held accountable for sins. And from it: "He broke (ḥanitha) his oath," in contrast to "he fulfilled (barra) it." It is said: "taḥannatha" when one commits sin and becomes scrupulous. A'a-ābā'unā: the interrogative hamza has entered upon the conjunction particle. If you ask: how is coordination with the pronoun in lamab'ūthūna good without emphasis by "naḥnu"? I say: it is good because of the intervening element, which is the hamza, just as it is good in His saying, "neither we nor our fathers had associated [anything]" (ﷻ), because of the emphatic negating particle lā. It has been read: aw ābā'unā. It has also been read: la-majmū'ūna (and the gathered ones) ilā mīqāti yawmin ma'lūmin (to the appointed time of a known day): to the time that the world was fixed for, a known day, and the idafa (construct) is in the sense of "min," like "a ring of silver." Al-mīqāt is that by which a thing is timed, i.e., its limit. From it come the mawāqīt al-iḥrām (the stations of ihram), which are the limits that one who wishes to enter Mecca may not pass except in the state of ihram.

Ayyuhā al-ḍāllūna (O you who went astray from guidance), al-mukadhdhibūna bil-ba'th (who deny the resurrection), and they are the people of Mecca and those in a similar condition. Min shajarin min zaqqūmin: the first min is for the beginning of the extent, and the second is to explain and specify the tree. He made the pronoun referring to the tree feminine according to the meaning, and masculine according to the wording, in His saying minhā and 'alayhi. Whoever reads min shajarin min zaqqūmin has made both pronouns refer to the tree, and the second was mentioned by way of interpreting zaqqūm, since it explains it and is of its meaning.

It is reported from Ja'far al-Ṣādiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he read it with fatḥa on the shīn, meaning "the act of drinking." As for the kasra, it means "that which is drunk," i.e., what the hīm drink. Al-hīm are camels afflicted with al-hiyām, a disease from which they drink and are never quenched. It is the plural of ahyam and hayma'. Dhu al-Rumma said:

"So she became like the hayma' (thirst-stricken camel), for neither cool water satisfies its thirst, nor is its longing ended."

[Dhu al-Rumma's verses, with commentary: "And Mayy provided us at the parting with a kiss, a long-lasting bond of needs, whose sickness is prolonged... So she became like the hayma', to which neither cool water brings relief... nor is its longing ended." He says: she provided us, i.e., made our provision Mayy's kiss at departure, and that kiss was the bond of needs and causes of longing for union. "'Alā'iqu" is a raised predicate or a accusative apposition. "Al-saqām" (sickness) is like kalām, and "suqm" like ta'ab, and "suqm" like bukhl, a verbal noun of saqima; i.e., its toil is long-lasting and does not heal. The camel is called ahyam and the she-camel hayma', when the hiyām afflicts them; it is a disease, caused by which the hearts of camels boil like extreme thirst. His saying "lā al-mā'u mubrad" is a resumptive clause explaining the point of similarity, or a circumstantial clause: water does not cool their thirst, nor is it ended for them, i.e., their longing does not stop, so I am likewise: no union that would heal me, nor does despair kill me. It is also narrated: "wa-lā yuqḍā 'alā hiyāmihā," and perhaps its meaning: neither water cools the burning that I have received from it, nor does the longing that I received from it kill me; but the first is more firmly established and better in meaning.]

It was also said: al-hīm are sands. Its basis is that it is the plural of al-hiyām with a fatḥa on the hā', which is sand that does not hold together, pluralized on the pattern fa'l like saḥāb and suḥb; then it was lightened and treated as the plural abyaḍ. The meaning: there is imposed upon them from hunger what compels them to eat the zaqqūm, which is like molten dregs. When they have filled their bellies from it, there is imposed upon them from thirst what compels them to drink the ḥamīm that cuts their intestines, so they drink it as the hīm drink water.

If you ask: how is the coordination of "drinkers" upon "drinkers" correct, when they are of the same subject and the same two attributes are identical, so that it would be coordinating a thing upon itself? From it come the mawāqīt al-iḥrām (the stations of ihram), which are the limits that one who wishes to enter Mecca may not pass except in the state of ihram.

Ayyuhā al-ḍāllūna (O you who went astray from guidance), al-mukadhdhibūna bil-ba'th (who deny the resurrection), and they are the people of Mecca and those in a similar condition. Min shajarin min zaqqūmin: the first min is for the beginning of the extent, and the second is to explain and specify the tree. He made the pronoun referring to the tree feminine according to the meaning, and masculine according to the wording, in His saying minhā and 'alayhi. Whoever reads min shajarin min zaqqūmin has made both pronouns refer to the tree, and the second was mentioned by way of interpreting zaqqūm, since it explains it and is of its meaning.

Shurba al-hīm (drinking as the thirsty camels drink). It has been read with the three vowel forms; the fatḥa and ḍamma are both verbal nouns (maṣdars). It is reported from Ja'far al-Ṣādiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he read it with fatḥa on the shīn, meaning "the act of drinking." As for the kasra, it means "that which is drunk," i.e., what the hīm drink. Al-hīm are camels afflicted with al-hiyām, a disease from which they drink and are never quenched. It is the plural of ahyam and hayma'. Dhu al-Rumma said:

"So she became like the hayma' (thirst-stricken camel), for neither cool water satisfies its thirst, nor is its longing ended."

[Dhu al-Rumma's verses, with commentary: "And Mayy provided us at the parting with a kiss, a long-lasting bond of needs, whose sickness is prolonged... So she became like the hayma', to which neither cool water brings relief... nor is its longing ended." He says: she provided us, i.e., made our provision Mayy's kiss at departure, and that kiss was the bond of needs and causes of longing for union. "'Alā'iqu" is a raised predicate or a accusative apposition. "Al-saqām" (sickness) is like kalām, and "suqm" like ta'ab, and "suqm" like bukhl, a verbal noun of saqima; i.e., its toil is long-lasting and does not heal. The camel is called ahyam and the she-camel hayma', when the hiyām afflicts them; it is a disease, caused by which the hearts of camels boil like extreme thirst. His saying "lā al-mā'u mubrad" is a resumptive clause explaining the point of similarity, or a circumstantial clause: water does not cool their thirst, nor is it ended for them, i.e., their longing does not stop, so I am likewise: no union that would heal me, nor does despair kill me. It is also narrated: "wa-lā yuqḍā 'alā hiyāmihā," and perhaps its meaning: neither water cools the burning that I have received from it, nor does the longing that I received from it kill me; but the first is more firmly established and better in meaning.]

It was also said: al-hīm are sands. Its basis is that it is the plural of al-hiyām with a fatḥa on the hā', which is sand that does not hold together, pluralized on the pattern fa'l like saḥāb and suḥb; then it was lightened and treated as the plural abyaḍ. The meaning: there is imposed upon them from hunger what compels them to eat the zaqqūm, which is like molten dregs. When they have filled their bellies from it, there is imposed upon them from thirst what compels them to drink the ḥamīm that cuts their intestines, so they drink it as the hīm drink water.

If you ask: how is the coordination of "drinkers" upon "drinkers" correct, when they are of the same subject and the same two attributes are identical, so that it would be coordinating a thing upon itself? I say: they are not identical, in that their being drinkers of the ḥamīm in the state it is in—extreme heat and cutting the intestines—is a strange matter, and their drinking it as the hīm drink water is also a strange matter; so they are two different attributes.

Nuzl: the provision prepared for a guest out of honor. There is mockery in it, as in His saying, "so give them the good news of a painful punishment" (ﷻ), and like the saying of Abū al-Shi'r al-Ḍabbī:

"And when the tyrant came upon us with his army, we made the spears and the sharp swords his nuzl (welcome)."

[The explanation of this witness has been given in the first part, p. 458; refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]

It has been read: nuzluhum with light pronunciation.

Why then do you not confirm? This is an exhortation to affirm (the truth): either regarding creation, for although they affirm it, their doctrine contradicts what affirming it requires, so it is as though they deny it; or regarding resurrection, for whoever created you at first cannot be prevented from creating again.

As for what you emit (ma tumnūn), that is, what you eject into the wombs as sperm drops. Abū al-Simāl read it with an opening tā' (tamnūn). It is said: amnā al-nuṭfa and manā al-nuṭfa (he emitted the drop). Allah the Exalted said: "from a drop when it is emitted" (min nuṭfatin idhā tumnā).

Do you create it (takhluqūnahu)? That is, do you determine it and form it.

We have decreed death among you (qaddarnā baynakumu al-mawt) as a decree, and We have distributed it upon you as the distribution of provision, with difference and variation as Our will requires, so your lifespans differed: short, long, and intermediate.

It was also read qaddarnā with light stress (takhfīf). To outstrip (sabaqa) something means: when you prevent someone from it, overpower him in it, and do not enable him to reach it. So the meaning of His words "And We are not to be outstripped (wa-mā naḥnu bi-masbūqīna) from replacing your likenesses (ʿalā an nubaddila amthālakum)" is: We are able to do that, and you cannot overpower Us in it. Amthālakum is the plural of mithl: that is, to replace from among you and in your place your counterparts from creation, "and to bring you into (wa-an nunshi'akum) a form you do not know and have not experienced the like of."

The meaning is: We are capable of both matters together, of creating what resembles you and what does not resemble you, so how could We be unable to restore you? It is also permissible that amthālakum be the plural of mithl, meaning: to replace and change your attributes which you possess in your creation and your characters, and to bring you into attributes you do not know.

The word al-nash'a was read also as al-nash'ā'a. In this there is evidence for the validity of analogy (qiyās), since He rebuked them for failing to analogize the second creation upon the first.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 56, verses 63–67:

﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾, i.e., the grain you scatter and the work you do in its ground. ﴿Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ You make it sprout and bring it forth as vegetation, [[His words "nabatan yarif wa yanma" (a plant that glistens and grows): in al-Sihah, "raffa lawnuhu yarifu" (with kasra) means it shone and sparkled. "Shajar rafif" means a tree whose leaves are moist. (A)]] that flourishes and grows until it reaches its completion. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

"None of you should say, 'I have sown (zara'tu),' but let him say, 'I have ploughed (harathtu).'" [[Narrated by Ibn Hibban, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani through the route of Makhlad ibn Husayn, from Hisham ibn Hassan, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, with this wording. He said: Then Abu Hurayrah recited, "Have you considered what you plough? Is it you who sow it?"]] Abu Hurayrah said: "Have you considered" [[His words "Abu Hurayrah said: Have you considered": he cited the verse as evidence for the hadith, namely the words of the Exalted, "Have you considered what you plough?" His words "Have you considered" is an address to those who hear him, and he meant the sense of looking, so he used "ila" after it, as in "Have they not looked at what Allah has created of any thing?" (A)]] the verse: ﴿Have you considered what you plough?﴾ ... the verse. Al-Hutam: from "hatama," like al-futat and al-judhadh from "fatta" and "jadhdha," which is that which has become dry stalks and crumbled. ﴿Then you would be left in wonder﴾ (fazaltum), and it is also read with kasra (fazilltum). Fazaltum is in its original form. ﴿Tafakkahun﴾ means you would be astonished. From al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "You would regret your toil in it and your expenditure upon it," or "regret the sins you committed, for which you were stricken by this." It is also read as "tafkanun." From it is the hadith: "The likeness of the scholar is like the hot spring (al-hummah) which the distant come to, and the near leave it. Then while they are thus, its water dries up, and a people benefit from it while another people remain, tafakkahun," [[His words "the likeness of the hummah which the distant come to": in al-Sihah, "al-hummah" is a hot spring by which the wealthy and the sick seek healing. In the hadith: "The scholar is like the hummah." (A)]] [[I have not found it.]] meaning: they will regret. ﴿Indeed, we are laden with debt﴾, i.e., obligated to bear the cost of what we spent, and ruined in the loss of our provision, from al-gharam, which is destruction. ﴿Rather, we are deprived﴾, i.e., destitute and cut off, having no share and no fortune. Had we been favoured by fortune, this would not have befallen us. It is also read as "a-inna."

**Question:** Why was the *lam* (the particle of emphasis) placed on the answer to *law* (if) in ﴿لَجَعَلْناهُ حُطاماً﴾ (We would surely have made it crumbled debris), and why is it omitted here?

**Answer:** *Law* (if) when it governs two clauses whose second clause is linked to the first, so that the consequent depends on the condition, is not like *in* (if) which purely marks the condition, nor does it work like *in*. The sense of the condition enters it incidentally, since it indicates that the second clause was prevented because the first was prevented. Therefore its answer needs something to mark this dependency. So this *lam* was added to serve as that marker. When it is then omitted, after it has become a well-known marker in its place, this is because a thing that is known, whose position is recognized, and which has become familiar, is not troubled by dropping it from the wording, relying on the listener's knowledge. Do you not see what is related about Ru'ba? He used to say "*khayr*" (well) to whoever asked him, "How are you?" He dropped the preposition because everyone knew where it belonged. Its omission and its presence were equal because the matter was so well known. And it is enough to cite the verse of Aws:

*Until, when the dogs were said to them,*
*"Like today, one is pursued and there is no pursuit."*

Its omission in "*lam ara*" (I did not see) is therefore a verbal abbreviation, while it remains present in meaning. So the two positions are equal with no difference between them. Moreover, its earlier mention and the short distance between the two make it unnecessary to mention it a second time, and it stands in for it. It may also be said that this *lam* certainly conveys emphasis. It was therefore inserted in the verse about food and not in the verse about drink, to show that the matter of food takes precedence over the matter of drink, and that the threat of losing it is more severe and harder, because drink is needed only as a follower of food. Do you not see that you give your guest water only after you have fed him? If the order were reversed, you would fall under the words of Abu al-'Ala':

*When they give the guests of people milk to drink,*
*they give their guests cold, pure water.*

[Editor's note: Abu al-'Ala' composed this praising Sa'd al-Dawla Abu al-Fada'il, and he was criticized because he praised giving guests water before mentioning food. *Al-makhd* (with two dotted letters) is milk whose butter has been removed, and it has the sense of *al-mamkhud*. It is also narrated as *mahdan* (with an undotted letter), meaning pure, either sweet or sour. *Al-shabm* (on the pattern of *hadhar*) means cold. *Al-zalal* means cold water. Here, since the scholars of rhetoric (*balagha*) gave the situation (*maqam*) a role in indicating the intended meaning, we say: the meaning of the verse is that when people hurry to give milk to their guests and are satisfied with it instead of hurrying to bring food, then they hurry to prepare food for their guests. Therefore, giving the guests water indicates that food was brought earlier, by the help of the situation, because this is customarily implied, so there is no fault in it.]

Some Arabs drank and said: "I do not drink except in one draught (*thumaylah*)." For this reason the verse about food was placed before the verse about drink.

تُورُونَ: تقدحونها وتستخرجونها من الزناد. والعرب تقدح بعودين، تحكّ أحدهما على الآخر، ويسمّون الأعلى: الزند، والأسفل: الزندة، شبهوهما بالفحل والطروقة [[قوله «بالفحل والطروقة» أنثى الفحل، كما في الصحاح. (ع)]].

شَجَرَتَها التي منها الزناد: تَذْكِرَةً تذكيرا لنار جهنم، حيث علقنا بها أسباب المعايش كلها، وعممنا بالحاجة إليها البلوى لتكون حاضرة للناس ينظرون إليها ويذكرون ما أُوعدوا به. أو جعلناها تذكرة وأنموذجا من جهنم، لما روي عن رسول الله (ﷺ): «ناركم هذه التي يوقد بنو آدم جزء من سبعين جزأ من حرّ جهنم» [[متفق عليه من حديث أبي هريرة.]].

وَمَتاعاً ومنفعة لِلْمُقْوِينَ: للذين ينزلون القواء، وهي القفر. أو للذين خلت بطونهم أو مزاودهم من الطعام. يقال: أقويت من أيام، أي لم آكل شيئا.

فَسَبِّحْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ: فأحدث التسبيح بذكر اسم ربك، أو أراد بالاسم: الذكر، أي: بذكر ربك. والْعَظِيمِ صفة للمضاف أو للمضاف إليه. والمعنى: أنه لما ذكر ما دل على قدرته وإنعامه على عباده قال: فأحدث التسبيح، وهو أن يقول: سبحان الله، إمّا تنزيها له عما يقول الظالمون الذين يجحدون وحدانيته ويكفرون نعمته، وإما تعجبا من أمرهم في غمط آلائه [[قوله «في غمط آلائه» أي تحقير نعمه. أفاده الصحاح. (ع)]] وأياديه الظاهرة، وإما شكرا لله على النعم التي عدّها ونبّه عليها.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 56, verse 75–80:

﴿فَلا أُقْسِمُ﴾ means "so I swear" (fa-uqsimu). The lā is a superfluous emphatic particle, like its use in ﴿لِئَلَّا يَعْلَمَ أَهْلُ الْكِتابِ﴾. Al-Hasan recited fa-la-uqsimu. [[Editor's note: His saying "We are nearer to him than you are" – the reason for placing this after what precedes it does not appear except by considering the order he mentioned, so let it be examined. (ʿ)]]

The meaning is: in your denial of God's acts and signs in everything, if He sends down a book that is miraculous, you say, "It is sorcery and fabrication." "The *rawḥ* is mercy, because it is like life for the one shown mercy." It was also said it means "remaining," that is, both of these are his together, namely eternal abiding along with provision and bliss. The *rayḥān* is provision.

The pronoun in ﴿أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ﴾ refers to the dying person. ﴿غَيْرَ مَدِينِينَ﴾ means "not subject to lordship (*marbūbīn*)," from *dāna al-sultān al-ra'iyya*, meaning the ruler governed his subjects. ﴿وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْكُمْ﴾ means "We are nearer to him than you are," that is, to the people of the deceased, by Our power and Our knowledge, or by the angels of death. [[Editor's note: His saying "We are nearer to him than you are" – the reason for placing this after what precedes it does not appear except by considering the order he mentioned, so let it be examined. (ʿ)]]

The meaning is: in your denial of God's acts and signs in everything, if He sends down a book that is miraculous, you say, "It is sorcery and fabrication." If He sends a messenger to you, you say, "He is a lying sorcerer." If He sends you rain by which He gives you life, you say, "It is the rising of such-and-such a star," following a doctrine that leads to neglect and nullification. So why do you not return the spirit to the body after it reaches the throat, if there is no one who takes it? And if you are truthful in your nullification and disbelief in the Giver of life, the Giver of death, the Originator and the Restorer?

As for ﴿فَأَمَّا إِنْ كَانَ الْمُتَوَفَّى مِنَ الْمُقَرَّبِينَ﴾, if the deceased is among those brought near, that is, among the foremost, from the three pairs mentioned at the beginning of the surah, then ﴿فَرَوْحٌ﴾ means he has rest. ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): *fa-rawḥ*, [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ishaq and al-Hakim, from the narration of Badil ibn Maysara from ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaqiq from ʿĀʾisha. Ishaq added "with the rāʾ pronounced with a ḍamma."]] with a *ḍamma*. al-Ḥasan also read it that way, and he said:

"The *rawḥ* is mercy, because it is like life for the one shown mercy." It was also said it means "remaining," that is, both of these are his together, namely eternal abiding along with provision and bliss. The *rayḥān* is provision.

﴿فَسَلَامٌ لَكَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الْيَمِينِ﴾ means: "Peace upon you, O companion of the right hand, from your brethren, the companions of the right hand," that is, they greet you with peace, as in His saying, ﴿إِلَّا قِيلًا سَلَامًا سَلَامًا﴾.

﴿فَنُزُلٌ مِنْ حَمِيمٍ﴾ is like His saying, ﴿هَذَا نُزُلُهُمْ يَوْمَ الدِّينِ﴾. It is also read with the lighter pronunciation. ﴿وَتَصْلِيَةُ جَحِيمٍ﴾ is read with the *raf'* and the *jarr*, as a conjunction to *nuzul* and *ḥamīm*. ﴿إِنَّ هَذَا لَهُوَ حَقُّ الْيَقِينِ﴾ means: the true certainty that is firmly established.

From the Messenger of Allah (may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family): "Whoever recites Surat al-Waqiʿa every night will never be afflicted with poverty." [[Narrated by Ibn Wahb in his *Jamiʿ*: "Al-Sarrī ibn Yaḥyā told me that Shujāʿ narrated to him from Abū Ẓabya from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿūd." Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥakīm and ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl al-Baṣrī both followed him, both from al-Sarrī. al-Bayhaqī narrated it in *al-Shuʿab* through both routes.

Abū Yaʿlā also narrated it from the narration of Muḥammad ibn Ḥabīb from al-Sarrī. al-Bayhaqī in *al-Shuʿab* narrated it from the narration of Ḥajjāj ibn Minhāl from al-Sarrī, saying: "From Shujāʿ from Ibn Fāṭima from Ibn Masʿūd." Likewise Abū ʿUbayd narrated it in *Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān* from the narration of al-Sarrī, saying: "From Abū Ẓabya." So the students of al-Sarrī differed over whether his teacher was Shujāʿ or Abū Shujāʿ. They also differed over Shujāʿ's teacher, whether he was Abū Fāṭima or Abū Ẓabya. Then they differed over the vocalization of Abū Ẓabya. According to al-Dāraquṭnī, it is with an unpointed *ṭāʾ* followed by a *yāʾ* with two dots below, then a *bāʾ*, and he is ʿĪsā ibn Sulaymān al-Jurjānī, and his narration from Ibn Masʿūd is disconnected (*munqaṭiʿ*). This is supported by al-Thaʿlabī narrating it through Abū Bakr al-ʿUṭāridī from al-Sarrī from Shujāʿ from Abū Ẓabya al-Jurjānī. According to al-Bayhaqī, it is with a dotted letter followed by a *bāʾ*, then a *yāʾ* with two dots below, and that he is unknown. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: "This is a munkar ḥadīth, and I do not know Shujāʿ."]]
